headline: GTA VI is out tomorrow. Miami paid $3.9M to play along.
summary: 'Grand Theft Auto VI' unlocks at midnight on Nov. 19, 13 years after the last one. It returns to Vice City, Rockstar's made-up Miami. The series has sold more than 470 million copies, and GTA V alone took $1 billion in three days. Miami-Dade County signed a $3.9 million deal to promote it, with a giant 'Welcome to Vice City' sign on the Heat's arena.

cover_question.q: Can I play it when it comes out?

cover_answer: No. Stealing cars and dodging police is a grown-up game.
table_question: Would you take money to advertise something you'd ban at home?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: A huge video game comes out tomorrow. Grown-ups have waited 13 years for it, longer than you have been alive. It's about stealing cars and running from the police, so it isn't for kids, the way some movies aren't. There are piles of games made for you, and this one isn't going anywhere.
5-7.why: The 13-year wait is the picture. The crime stays a label.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them the wait, longer than their own life, and leaves the crime as a label like a movie rating. They read your face before your words, so say it flat. Expect 'but my friend plays it.' Maybe. In our house it's a grown-up game.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: GTA V took $1 billion in three days in 2013. Rockstar spent 13 years on the sequel, set in a made-up Miami. Miami-Dade County paid $3.9 million to promote it, and some officials asked why public money should sell a crime game. A school sponsoring a movie it won't let you watch.
8-12.why: A chain that ends in a fairness call.
8-12.why_long: At twelve a child is testing whether adults apply their own rules, so the script runs the chain: a record hit, a 13-year sequel, a county paying to be in the picture, officials objecting. The school-and-movie line is the fairness call. Expect 'so is the game bad or not?' The AP says players love the freedom and critics flag the violence.

13-17.script: Should a county spend $3.9 million promoting a game about crime? Miami-Dade did, the Heat will wear 'Vice City' jerseys, and some officials objected. Second: Rockstar hired real gang members to voice characters in earlier games. Does that make it more honest, or only easier to sell?
13-17.why_long: A thirteen-year-old can hold two true things: critics fault its violence and how it treats women, and 470 million copies say people want it. The script asks whether a city should profit from that and whether hiring real gang members is honesty or marketing. Expect 'you played it, didn't you?' Answer straight; they test whether you argue honestly.

5-7.q: Can I play it when it comes out?
5-7.a: No. It's about stealing cars and running from police. Grown-ups waited 13 years for it. You can wait longer.

8-12.a: The AP piece doesn't say. Rockstar promises its biggest world yet.

8-12.q: Why would a city pay to be in a crime game?
8-12.a: Attention. Miami-Dade paid $3.9 million. Some officials objected.

13-17.q: Is it wrong for a city to advertise a crime game?
13-17.a: Miami-Dade bet $3.9 million the attention pays. Officials split. Your call.

13-17.q: Why do people love a game about crime?
13-17.a: The AP credits the freedom to roam. Critics flag the violence. Both true.

caption:
No. Stealing cars and dodging police is a grown-up game.
